Bernstein Polynomial

Documents/Bernstein Polynomial

The package stores parameter-dependent matrices with cell-local Bernstein coefficients. This chapter explains the mathematical facts used by pdmat, pdvar, rhodiff, and pdlmi. Each API page places validation and implemented input and validation boundaries beside the call they affect.

For a diagram-led walkthrough of the actual one- and two-dimensional input shapes, cell traversal, and the distinction between physical gridding and Bernstein Degree, see Gridding And Bernstein Degree.

Begin With One Polynomial

Section titled “Begin With One Polynomial”

Take the ordinary polynomial

p(α)=1+2α+3α2,α∈[0,1].p(\alpha)=1+2\alpha+3\alpha^2, \qquad \alpha\in[0,1].p(α)=1+2α+3α2,α∈[0,1].

The same polynomial in the degree-two Bernstein basis is

p(α)=1B02(α)+2B12(α)+6B22(α).p(\alpha)=1B_0^2(\alpha)+2B_1^2(\alpha)+6B_2^2(\alpha).p(α)=1B02​(α)+2B12​(α)+6B22​(α).

The coefficient row [1, 2, 6] is another exact representation of the polynomial. These are not three new physical grid nodes and are not, in general, three sampled values. The package applies the same change of basis to full matrices on every physical cell.

From 1912 To Parameter-Dependent LMIs

Section titled “From 1912 To Parameter-Dependent LMIs”

Bernstein introduced the basis in 1912 for a constructive proof of the Weierstrass approximation theorem. The same control-point form later became the basis of Bezier curves and the de Casteljau evaluation and subdivision algorithm. Farouki’s centennial retrospective surveys that history, the basis properties, and its numerical algorithms.

The bridge to PD-LMIs is not approximation alone. On a physical parameter cell, nonnegative basis functions that sum to one make a scalar, vector, or matrix polynomial a convex combination of finitely many coefficient objects. Exact coefficient multiplication, differentiation, and degree elevation then let the package assemble local matrix expressions before pdlmi forms finite sufficient constraints.

Local Coordinate, Basis Order, And Endpoint Labels

Section titled “Local Coordinate, Basis Order, And Endpoint Labels”

On one-dimensional physical cell ccc, with endpoints [ρ1(c),ρ1(c+1)][\rho_1^{(c)},\rho_1^{(c+1)}][ρ1(c)​,ρ1(c+1)​], the package uses

α=ρ−ρ1(c)ρ1(c+1)−ρ1(c),α∈[0,1].\alpha = \frac{\rho-\rho_1^{(c)}}{\rho_1^{(c+1)}-\rho_1^{(c)}}, \qquad \alpha \in [0,1].α=ρ1(c+1)​−ρ1(c)​ρ−ρ1(c)​​,α∈[0,1].

The scalar degree-mmm basis is

Bim(α)=(mi)(1−α)m−iαi,i=0,…,m.B_i^m(\alpha) = \binom{m}{i}(1-\alpha)^{m-i}\alpha^i, \qquad i=0,\ldots,m.Bim​(α)=(im​)(1−α)m−iαi,i=0,…,m.

Thus labels run from left to right in the standard order. Before normalization, the ordered factor pattern is

(1−α)m,(1−α)m−1α,…,αm.(1-\alpha)^m,\quad (1-\alpha)^{m-1}\alpha,\quad \ldots,\quad \alpha^m.(1−α)m,(1−α)m−1α,…,αm.

The normalized Bernstein basis factors include the binomial coefficients (mi)\binom{m}{i}(im​) shown in the definition above. The endpoint labels are:

  • at the left endpoint ρ=ρ1(c)\rho=\rho_1^{(c)}ρ=ρ1(c)​, α=0\alpha=0α=0 and local label 0 is selected;
  • at the right endpoint ρ=ρ1(c+1)\rho=\rho_1^{(c+1)}ρ=ρ1(c+1)​, α=1\alpha=1α=1 and local label m is selected.

For degree two,

P(c)(α)=(1−α)2C(c)[0]+2(1−α)αC(c)[1]+α2C(c)[2].P^{(c)}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^2C^{(c)}[0] +2(1-\alpha)\alpha C^{(c)}[1]+\alpha^2C^{(c)}[2].P(c)(α)=(1−α)2C(c)[0]+2(1−α)αC(c)[1]+α2C(c)[2].

On physical cell ccc, write the stored objects as C(c)[0],C(c)[1],C(c)[2]C^{(c)}[0],C^{(c)}[1],C^{(c)}[2]C(c)[0],C(c)[1],C(c)[2]. The package stores them as coefficient matrices or expressions. It does not treat them as arbitrary samples of a fitted curve. A function-only pdmat constructed without explicit Degree is different: it retains its exact function handle but does not claim Bernstein coefficient evidence.

Nonnegativity, Unit Sum, And Convex Hulls

Section titled “Nonnegativity, Unit Sum, And Convex Hulls”

For α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]α∈[0,1],

Bim(α)≥0,∑i=0mBim(α)=1.B_i^m(\alpha)\ge 0, \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{m}B_i^m(\alpha)=1.Bim​(α)≥0,i=0∑m​Bim​(α)=1.

Therefore

P(c)(α)=∑iBim(α)P(c)[i]P^{(c)}(\alpha)=\sum_i B_i^m(\alpha)P^{(c)}[i]P(c)(α)=i∑​Bim​(α)P(c)[i]

lies in the convex hull of its coefficients. The statement applies to several payload types:

  • scalar: min⁡iP(c)[i]≤P(c)(α)≤max⁡iP(c)[i]\min_i P^{(c)}[i]\le P^{(c)}(\alpha)\le\max_iP^{(c)}[i]mini​P(c)[i]≤P(c)(α)≤maxi​P(c)[i];
  • vector: every value lies in the convex hull of the coefficient vectors;
  • matrix: every value is a convex combination of the coefficient matrices.

For symmetric matrix coefficients, if every P(c)[i]⪯0P^{(c)}[i]\preceq0P(c)[i]⪯0, then P(c)(α)⪯0P^{(c)}(\alpha)\preceq0P(c)(α)⪯0 throughout the cell. Apply the scalar convex-combination argument to xTP(c)(α)xx^{\mathsf T}P^{(c)}(\alpha)xxTP(c)(α)x for every vector xxx. Strictly negative coefficient matrices similarly give a strict cell-wide certificate.

The converse does not generally hold. A matrix polynomial can be negative definite everywhere while one or more Bernstein coefficient matrices fail the same sign test. Coefficient-wise matrix sign conditions are therefore safe but potentially conservative; failure of the finite test does not prove that the continuous PD-LMI is infeasible.

Tensor Products On Hyperrectangles

Section titled “Tensor Products On Hyperrectangles”

For ℓ\ellℓ scheduling dimensions, the package uses the tensor-product basis

Bim(α)=∏r=1ℓBirmr(αr).B_{\mathbf{i}}^{\mathbf{m}}(\boldsymbol\alpha) =\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}B_{i_r}^{m_r}(\alpha_r).Bim​(α)=r=1∏ℓ​Bir​mr​​(αr​).

The products remain nonnegative and sum to one, so the convex-hull and matrix sign arguments hold on every physical hyperrectangle. Bernstein bases on simplices are related, but simplex storage is not the pdbase convention. Here each axis has an independent grid interval and local label.

The tensor picture deliberately uses four physical nodes on the first axis and three on the second: axis node counts need not match. In ℓ\ellℓ dimensions, a physical node has multi-index j=(j1,…,jℓ)\mathbf j=(j_1,\ldots,j_\ell)j=(j1​,…,jℓ​) and coordinates ρ(j)=(ρ1(j1),…,ρℓ(jℓ))\boldsymbol\rho^{(\mathbf j)}=(\rho_1^{(j_1)},\ldots,\rho_\ell^{(j_\ell)})ρ(j)=(ρ1(j1​)​,…,ρℓ(jℓ​)​). A cell has identity c\mathbf cc, and a local Bernstein label is i=(i1,…,iℓ)\mathbf i=(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)i=(i1​,…,iℓ​). A stored matrix is therefore C(c)[i]C^{(\mathbf c)}[\mathbf i]C(c)[i].

LocalValues, Continuity, And Boundaries

Section titled “LocalValues, Continuity, And Boundaries”

Physical cells are stored as a nested tree:

Each selected leaf is a flat coefficient cell in combination order over the local labels. Grid normalization happens independently on each physical cell, so nonuniform cell widths are supported and labels describe local basis positions rather than global node numbers.

Continuous pdvar objects share symbolic coefficient handles across common cell faces. Continuity is thus encoded in the coefficient graph rather than by extra equality LMIs. Cell-local derivative objects are deliberately different: their boundary rows stay separate because neighboring cells can have different physical widths and different partial-difference data.

Differentiation

Section titled “Differentiation”

For

P(c)(α)=∑i=0mP(c)[i]Bim(α),P^{(c)}(\alpha)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}P^{(c)}[i]B_i^m(\alpha),P(c)(α)=i=0∑m​P(c)[i]Bim​(α),

the forward coordinate gives the physical derivative on one-dimensional cell ccc of width hc=ρ1(c+1)−ρ1(c)h_c=\rho_1^{(c+1)}-\rho_1^{(c)}hc​=ρ1(c+1)​−ρ1(c)​:

dP(c)dρ=mhc∑i=0m−1(P(c)[i+1]−P(c)[i])Bim−1(α).\frac{dP^{(c)}}{d\rho} =\frac{m}{h_c}\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} \bigl(P^{(c)}[i+1]-P^{(c)}[i]\bigr)B_i^{m-1}(\alpha).dρdP(c)​=hc​m​i=0∑m−1​(P(c)[i+1]−P(c)[i])Bim−1​(α).

For several parameters, P˙=∑r(∂P/∂ρr)ρ˙r\dot P=\sum_r(\partial P/\partial\rho_r)\dot\rho_rP˙=∑r​(∂P/∂ρr​)ρ˙​r​. rhodiff forms the cell-local partial differences, aligns tensor degrees as required, and stores one row for each active rate-box vertex. The rhodiff reference documents the supported call forms and validation rules.

Degree Elevation For Any Target Degree

Section titled “Degree Elevation For Any Target Degree”

A degree-mmm polynomial can be represented exactly at any degree M≥mM\ge mM≥m. For one parameter, the package-indexed coefficients are

C^(c)[k]=∑i=max⁡(0,k−(M−m))min⁡(m,k)C(c)[i] (mi)(M−mk−i)(Mk),k=0,…,M.\widehat C^{(c)}[k]= \sum_{i=\max(0,k-(M-m))}^{\min(m,k)} C^{(c)}[i]\, \frac{\binom{m}{i}\binom{M-m}{k-i}}{\binom{M}{k}}, \qquad k=0,\ldots,M.C(c)[k]=i=max(0,k−(M−m))∑min(m,k)​C(c)[i](kM​)(im​)(k−iM−m​)​,k=0,…,M.

Tensor products apply the same elevation along every parameter direction. Elevation preserves the represented polynomial and introduces no new decision freedom. It is used to align compatible coefficient-backed operands of different degrees. This must not be confused with constructing a genuinely higher-degree decision parameterization, which enlarges the search space.

de Casteljau Evaluation And Exact Subdivision

Section titled “de Casteljau Evaluation And Exact Subdivision”

The de Casteljau recursion repeatedly forms affine combinations:

C(r)[j]=(1−α)C(r−1)[j]+αC(r−1)[j+1],C(0)[j]=C(c)[j].C^{(r)}[j]=(1-\alpha)C^{(r-1)}[j]+\alpha C^{(r-1)}[j+1], \qquad C^{(0)}[j]=C^{(c)}[j].C(r)[j]=(1−α)C(r−1)[j]+αC(r−1)[j+1],C(0)[j]=C(c)[j].

It evaluates the polynomial stably, and the two edge chains of its recursion triangle provide the exact Bernstein coefficients on the two subintervals at the split point. Tensor-product subdivision applies this one-dimensional operation one axis at a time.

Subdivision is relevant to certificates because re-expressing the same polynomial on smaller physical cells usually tightens the local coefficient convex hulls. The package does not currently expose a general public de Casteljau or adaptive-subdivision API; this section records background, not a call users can make today.

Product Degree And Coefficient Convolution

Section titled “Product Degree And Coefficient Convolution”

Basic idea

Section titled “Basic idea”

Multiplication creates every ordered pair of input coefficients. Pairs with the same label sum k=i+jk=i+jk=i+j contribute to the same output coefficient. The product degree is the sum of the input degrees; no extra physical grid nodes are created.

Formula

Section titled “Formula”

On a fixed physical cell, let

P(c)(α)=∑i=0mBim(α)P(c)[i],Q(c)(α)=∑j=0nBjn(α)Q(c)[j].\begin{aligned} P^{(c)}(\alpha)&=\sum_{i=0}^{m}B_i^m(\alpha)P^{(c)}[i],\\ Q^{(c)}(\alpha)&=\sum_{j=0}^{n}B_j^n(\alpha)Q^{(c)}[j]. \end{aligned}P(c)(α)Q(c)(α)​=i=0∑m​Bim​(α)P(c)[i],=j=0∑n​Bjn​(α)Q(c)[j].​

The basis-product identity is

BimBjn=(mi)(nj)(m+ni+j)Bi+jm+n,B_i^mB_j^n= \frac{\binom mi\binom nj}{\binom{m+n}{i+j}}B_{i+j}^{m+n},Bim​Bjn​=(i+jm+n​)(im​)(jn​)​Bi+jm+n​,

so the arbitrary-degree weighted convolution is

R(c)[k]=∑i+j=kP(c)[i]Q(c)[j](mi)(nj)(m+nk),k=0,…,m+n.R^{(c)}[k]=\sum_{i+j=k} P^{(c)}[i]Q^{(c)}[j] \frac{\binom{m}{i}\binom{n}{j}}{\binom{m+n}{k}}, \qquad k=0,\ldots,m+n.R(c)[k]=i+j=k∑​P(c)[i]Q(c)[j](km+n​)(im​)(jn​)​,k=0,…,m+n.

Microexample: quadratic times affine

Section titled “Microexample: quadratic times affine”

Take P=[1,2,6]P=[1,2,6]P=[1,2,6] and Q=[2,4]Q=[2,4]Q=[2,4]. The four anti-diagonal groups give

R[0]=2,R[1]=4,R[2]=283,R[3]=24.R[0]=2,\qquad R[1]=4,\qquad R[2]=\frac{28}{3},\qquad R[3]=24.R[0]=2,R[1]=4,R[2]=328​,R[3]=24.

These are four cubic Bernstein coefficients, not four point samples.

Visual conclusion

Section titled “Visual conclusion”

For tensor-product parameters, labels add componentwise, coefficient tensors convolve over every matching label pair, and the scale is the product of the one-dimensional binomial ratios. Matrix multiplication order is preserved: P(c)[i]Q(c)[j]P^{(c)}[i]Q^{(c)}[j]P(c)[i]Q(c)[j] cannot generally be exchanged with Q(c)[j]P(c)[i]Q^{(c)}[j]P^{(c)}[i]Q(c)[j]P(c)[i].

This direct coefficient convolution is implemented by the shared Bernstein backend and exercised by coefficient-backed pdmat algebra and supported known-data/pdvar products. It is representation algebra, not a relaxation. The supported decision boundary is equally important: known or numeric data may multiply one affine pdvar from either side, while decision-by-decision products and rate-dependent-by-decision products are rejected because they would leave the implemented affine model class.

Weighted Value-Grid Convolution

Section titled “Weighted Value-Grid Convolution”

The same product rule can be evaluated as an ordinary ordered ℓ\ellℓ-dimensional discrete convolution. Within one physical cell, reshape the flat coefficient lists into value grids indexed by coefficient multi-indices p∈{0,…,m}ℓ\mathbf p\in\{0,\ldots,m\}^{\ell}p∈{0,…,m}ℓ and q∈{0,…,n}ℓ\mathbf q\in\{0,\ldots,n\}^{\ell}q∈{0,…,n}ℓ, preserving the package’s lbls order. First restore the binomial weights carried by the tensor Bernstein basis:

A~p=Ap∏r=1ℓ(mpr),B~q=Bq∏r=1ℓ(nqr).\widetilde A_{\mathbf p} =A_{\mathbf p} \prod_{r=1}^{\ell}\binom{m}{p_r}, \qquad \widetilde B_{\mathbf q} =B_{\mathbf q} \prod_{r=1}^{\ell}\binom{n}{q_r}.Ap​=Ap​r=1∏ℓ​(pr​m​),Bq​=Bq​r=1∏ℓ​(qr​n​).

Next convolve the two weighted value grids over all componentwise label sums:

C~κ=(A~∗ℓB~)κ=∑p+q=κA~pB~q.\widetilde C_{\boldsymbol\kappa} =\bigl(\widetilde A *_\ell \widetilde B\bigr)_{\boldsymbol\kappa} =\sum_{\mathbf p+\mathbf q=\boldsymbol\kappa} \widetilde A_{\mathbf p}\widetilde B_{\mathbf q}.Cκ​=(A∗ℓ​B)κ​=p+q=κ∑​Ap​Bq​.

Finally remove the degree-(m+n)(m+n)(m+n) Bernstein weights to recover the stored coefficients:

Cκ=C~κ∏r=1ℓ(m+nκr).C_{\boldsymbol\kappa} =\frac{\widetilde C_{\boldsymbol\kappa}} {\displaystyle\prod_{r=1}^{\ell}\binom{m+n}{\kappa_r}}.Cκ​=r=1∏ℓ​(κr​m+n​)Cκ​​.

These three steps are algebraically equivalent to the binomial-scaled formula above. The product has common tensor Degree m+nm+nm+n and each physical cell has (m+n+1)ℓ(m+n+1)^{\ell}(m+n+1)ℓ coefficients. For matrix-valued grids, the convolution is ordered: every term is A~pB~q\widetilde A_{\mathbf p}\widetilde B_{\mathbf q}Ap​Bq​ in that left-to-right matrix order. The coefficient labels follow the same forward-coordinate endpoint order throughout; only binomial weights are temporarily restored and removed.

Hypercube Counts And Traversal

Section titled “Hypercube Counts And Traversal”

With axis node counts k1,…,kℓk_1,\ldots,k_\ellk1​,…,kℓ​, the number of physical hypercubes is

Ncell=∏s=1ℓ(ks−1).N_{\mathrm{cell}}=\prod_{s=1}^{\ell}(k_s-1).Ncell​=s=1∏ℓ​(ks​−1).

For a common local degree mmm, each hypercube stores (m+1)ℓ(m+1)^\ell(m+1)ℓ coefficients. More generally, a degree vector m\mathbf mm would have ∏r(mr+1)\prod_r(m_r+1)∏r​(mr​+1) tensor labels. The implemented package stores one scalar degree property and enumerates both physical cells and labels lexicographically, with earlier dimensions varying more slowly.

Direct Matrix Certificates

Section titled “Direct Matrix Certificates”

For a residual

Ec(α)=∑iBim(α)E(c)[i],E_c(\boldsymbol\alpha)= \sum_{\mathbf i}B_{\mathbf i}^{m}(\boldsymbol\alpha)E^{(c)}[\mathbf i],Ec​(α)=i∑​Bim​(α)E(c)[i],

the implemented pdlmi path creates one YALMIP sign constraint for every physical cell, local coefficient, and active rate-vertex row. Requiring all E(c)[i]⪯0E^{(c)}[\mathbf i]\preceq0E(c)[i]⪯0 is sufficient for the whole local matrix polynomial to be nonpositive. toYalmip then hands the finite constraint array to ordinary YALMIP solver calls.

The package does not currently expose a strictness-margin option. Users should not infer numerical strictness semantics beyond the constraints actually assembled by YALMIP.

Fixed-Order Putinar Box Certificate

Section titled “Fixed-Order Putinar Box Certificate”

The opt-in applyPutinar path is dimension-aware. In one parameter it dispatches to the same parity-specific Markov–Lukács form as the full-box selector, with minimum and default order ⌊m/2⌋\lfloor m/2\rfloor⌊m/2⌋. In two or more parameters it replaces coefficient-wise sign tests with an unweighted Bernstein-Gram term plus one αs(1−αs)\alpha_s(1-\alpha_s)αs​(1−αs​)-weighted term per axis. At absolute order r≥⌈m/2⌉r\ge\lceil m/2\rceilr≥⌈m/2⌉, those terms use tensor basis degrees r1r\mathbf1r1 and r1−esr\mathbf1-\mathbf e_sr1−es​, respectively. Exact coefficient identities are matched at tensor degree 2r12r\mathbf12r1 independently for every physical cell and rate row.

For two or more parameters, this is the implemented Putinar specialization for the local parameter box. It is not a general-domain or general-generator interface, does not search orders automatically, and does not insert a strictness margin or call a solver.

Fixed-Order Full Box Preordering

Section titled “Fixed-Order Full Box Preordering”

The opt-in applyFullBoxPreorder path replaces coefficient-wise sign tests with a cell-local Bernstein-Gram representation. It uses the parity-specific Markov-Lukács form in one parameter and every subset product of the box generators αs(1−αs)\alpha_s(1-\alpha_s)αs​(1−αs​) in multiple parameters. PSD Gram blocks are independent across physical cells and rate rows, and exact identities match the represented polynomial coefficients.

This is a fixed-order certificate on the local parameter box. In one parameter it is the same Markov–Lukács assembly selected by Putinar. In two or more parameters it is distinct from the Putinar box module because it includes every generator-subset product. It is not a general-domain SOS interface or an automatically selected hierarchy. The dedicated method page documents order selection, constraint ordering, relation signs, examples, and errors.

Four Different Refinements

Section titled “Four Different Refinements”

When a direct coefficient test fails, keep these operations distinct:

  1. Pure degree elevation re-expresses the same polynomial with different coefficients and no new decision variables.
  2. Physical subdivision or grid refinement restricts and reparameterizes the same polynomial on smaller cells, often tightening local convex hulls.
  3. Higher decision degree changes the decision-function parameterization and enlarges the search space.
  4. A relaxation hierarchy changes the sufficient certificate, usually by adding multipliers, slack variables, or another positivity construction.

The current package implements degree alignment and common-grid coefficient algebra, but does not expose an adaptive certificate-refinement workflow or a general public subdivision command. Constructor-created pdvar objects accept every finite nonnegative integer degree; supported products can raise the stored degree further.

Control Literature And Scope

Section titled “Control Literature And Scope”

The following references give context without becoming runtime dependencies:

  • Farouki (2012): historical development, basis properties, degree elevation, and de Casteljau algorithms.
  • Zettler and Garloff (1998): multivariate Bernstein expansion, positivity tests, and convex-hull value bounds for interval-parameter polynomial families.
  • Masubuchi, Kume, and Shimemura (1998): spline-type finite conditions and parameter-partition refinement for parameter-dependent LMIs under the paper’s assumptions.
  • Xu and Jabbari (2024): recent grid/spline LPV output-feedback synthesis and improved L2L_2L2​-gain context.
  • Chesi (2010): a broader survey of LMI techniques for optimization over polynomials in control.

These papers motivate the representation and certificate landscape. They do not imply that every theorem, refinement, or hierarchy in that literature is implemented in the MATLAB/YALMIP package. In particular, general SOS assembly, adaptive refinement, package-owned strictness or residual certification, and diagnostics remain reserved or unsupported. The supported SOS-family features are the fixed-order Putinar box and full box preordering certificates.
